<reason>Both sides were skilled and epistemically clean, but PRO built the more complete path. B's honor-vs-memory distinction framed the entire debate and was never dislodged; A's counter (honor is conferred once at naming, not daily) was crisp but mostly asserted against B's "inertia is a choice" and dead-hand-veto framing. B's Rebuttal 1 exposed a genuine tension in A's case (names heavy with meaning when removed, weightless when kept), forcing A onto defense. Most decisively, A's direct answers to B's pressure questions conceded (1) some names should come down without military defeat and (2) the Washington/Confederate difference is real — and B's closing converted those concessions into the motion's premises: the "undrawable" line was one A drew themselves. A's fallback (rename only after "genuine rupture") was asserted, not defended, and sat awkwardly with A's absolute-continuity opening. A did land a sharp fork on democratic keep-votes, exposing softness in B's "the motion has done its work" answer, but B partially repaired it by noting founders survive the "primarily" test. B also supplied a concrete line-drawing mechanism (defining public act plus dedication record), while A's "primarily is a permission slip" remained mostly a worry about future misuse. Format compliance was strong on both sides.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 "trap" — A1.2/A1.3 insist names orient and carry the city's memory while A1.6 insists letters on a lintel teach nothing — combined with the closing harvest of A4.1 (dictator's avenue is "propaganda, not inheritance") and A4.3 ("the historical difference is real"), which showed A had conceded the line-drawing the whole case denied was possible.</best_rebuttal>
